The Caucasian scraper Capoeta capoeta is a rheophilic cyprinid endemic to the Kura and Araxes river systems of the South Caucasus, where it occupies swift-flowing gravel-bed streams and upper reaches of larger rivers. Maximum size estimates for this species are derived from photographic records of trophy specimens; a particularly large individual measured 46.7 cm [Li = 46.7 cm] in fork length, which corresponds to a total length of 50 cm based on examination of the same image. This ultimate length places Capoeta capoeta among the larger members of its genus, likely reflecting the productive lotic habitats it inhabits. Growth increments in this species become increasingly marginal after the onset of maturity, and individuals in the wild may require over half a decade to approach such dimensions under prevailing thermal regimes.

Sexual maturation in this cyprinid exhibits a marked dimorphism in body size at the onset of puberty. Females from wild populations reach the pubertal threshold at a fork length of 20.9 cm [Lp = 20.9 cm], a value that corresponds to the initiation of vitellogenesis and the first detectable gonadal recrudescence. Males, in contrast, attain puberty at a considerably smaller body size, with the onset of spermatogenesis recorded at a fork length of 16.9 cm [Lp = 16.9 cm], indicating that males invest less in somatic growth before transitioning to reproductive function. This pattern is common among cyprinids where male reproductive success depends more on access to spawning grounds than on body size per se.

Reproductive output in Capoeta capoeta has been quantified from a gravid female with a fork length of 40.2 cm held at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the female produced approximately 35,859 eggs [N_R_i = approximately 35,859 eggs] over the course of the spawning season, with 1 annual spawning event [F_R_i = 1 annual spawning event] recorded for individuals of this size. The fecundity value is substantial, reflecting the large body cavity available for ovarian development in this potamodromous species, which undertakes upstream migrations to spawn on clean gravel substrates. Egg diameter was measured at 1.7 mm, and from this dimension the wet weight of a freshly fertilized egg was calculated as 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams] using the standard spherical volume formula. Such small egg mass is typical of cyprinids producing large numbers of pelagic or semi-pelagic eggs that develop in the interstitial spaces of gravel substrates.

Lifespan data for Capoeta capoeta come from mark-recapture studies conducted at an ambient water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] in the lower Kura River system. The oldest individual documented in this survey was estimated to be 12 years [am = 12 years] old, providing a benchmark for the species' longevity under natural lotic conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a cyprinid of its body size, likely a consequence of the seasonal predictability of flow regimes in its native drainage, which reduces the frequency of catastrophic mortality events. The relationship between environmental temperature and longevity is further underscored by the observation that captive individuals maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] consistently achieve ages approaching the 12-year mark (12 years) [am = 12 years], suggesting that thermal conditions rather than genetic constraints set the upper boundary of the lifespan.

Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that the growth trajectory of Capoeta capoeta is relatively slow, consistent with its occupation of cool, well-oxygenated montane streams. The 16.9 cm [Lp = 16.9 cm] fork length at puberty for males is similar to that reported for Capoeta tinca from Anatolia, while the 20.9 cm [Lp = 20.9 cm] fork length at puberty for females is somewhat larger, possibly reflecting the need for greater abdominal capacity to accommodate the large egg complement observed in gravid individuals of 40.2 cm fork length. The 0.0026 gram [Wwb = 0.0026 gram] wet weight at birth places the hatchling at the smaller end of the range for cyprinids, a trait that facilitates rapid yolk absorption and early transition to exogenous feeding in productive gravel-bed habitats. The 46.7 cm [Li = 46.7 cm] ultimate fork length appears to represent a true asymptotic size, as growth increments in specimens exceeding this dimension are negligible, and the 12-year maximum lifespan (12 years) [am = 12 years] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] provides sufficient time for most individuals to reach this plateau before senescence.
